A distributed ledger is a digital record-keeping system shared across multiple participants, with no single authority controlling the entire database.

 Decentralization
  Instead of one central server storing all records, every participant (called a node) maintains an identical copy of the ledger. When a new record is added, it is broadcast to the network, and each node updates its copy independently. This removes the need for a trusted intermediary to verify transactions.

 Immutability
  Records are grouped into blocks, and each block contains a cryptographic reference to the previous block. This creates a chain-like structure where altering any historical record would break the cryptographic link and be immediately detected by the other nodes. Once a record is accepted by the network, it becomes practically impossible to change retroactively.

 Consensus
  Because there is no central authority, the network must agree on which records are valid before adding them. Nodes follow a predefined protocol to reach agreement. Common mechanisms include proof-of-work, where nodes solve computational puzzles to earn the right to add the next block, and proof-of-stake, where the right to validate is weighted by the amount of resources a node has committed to the network.

Together, these three componentsdecentralization, immutability, and consensusallow strangers to maintain a shared, trustworthy record without relying on a central institution.
